A coquette is a woman who flirts with men to win their attention and admiration — but with no real intention of committing to them. She enjoys being desired and chased. The relationship itself doesn't interest her much; the thrill of being wanted does.

Think of a coquette as a woman who has mastered the art of attraction and uses it deliberately — not to fall in love, but to feel admired. She knows she is appealing, and she uses that awareness as a tool.

What makes her a coquette specifically, rather than just a friendly or charming person, is that she plays a game — consciously or as second nature. She sends signals that pull someone toward her, then cools off just enough to keep them guessing. She might give you a warm, lingering smile, make you feel like you're the most interesting person in the room, and then effortlessly shift her attention to someone else — leaving you wondering whether she likes you or not. That uncertainty is not an accident. It is, in fact, the entire point.

Her toolkit includes things like: holding eye contact a moment too long, then glancing away; being playful and warm one day, mysteriously distant the next; offering just enough encouragement to keep someone hopeful, but never enough to make them feel secure. She keeps her admirers in a kind of pleasant suspense.

It helps to understand a coquette by separating her from similar ideas:

She is not simply a flirt. A flirt might be playful and charming without any real strategy behind it — it's often just a personality trait. A coquette, on the other hand, is more deliberate. There is a consciousness to what she does.

She is not a seductress. A seductress is actively trying to draw someone into a romantic or sexual relationship. A coquette isn't really after that. She wants the pursuit, the attention, the admiration — not necessarily what comes after.

She is not necessarily cruel. This is important. A coquette is not a villain. She may genuinely enjoy people's company. She may not even realize the effect she has on others. Sometimes the behavior is calculated; sometimes it is simply her natural way of moving through the world. Either way, the word carries a mild criticism — it implies she is a little self-centered in romantic situations, a bit of a tease — but it is not a harsh insult. It is more knowing than angry.

"Coquette" carries a slightly old-fashioned, literary elegance to it. When someone calls a woman a coquette, it often has a tone of wry amusement — like you are recognizing a familiar type. It acknowledges her charm even as it gently calls out her game. You might admire a coquette's social grace while also pitying the poor souls she leaves confused in her wake.
Who Does the Word Refer To?

Traditionally and most commonly, "coquette" refers to a woman. The word is strongly associated with femininity in its classical usage. While in modern writing you might occasionally see it applied to a man, that remains rare and would feel unusual to most readers. When it is applied to men, it often signals that the writer is being deliberately playful or literary.

"She was a natural coquette — she never said anything outright, but somehow every man in the room left feeling like he had a chance."

"He had been taken in by her coquette's smile, never realizing she had no interest in any of them beyond the pleasure of their attention."

"For all her charm, she was a coquette at heart — she loved the beginning of things, the spark, the interest — but the moment someone fell for her completely, she was already looking elsewhere."

If you had to lock the meaning into a single sentence: a coquette is a woman who uses flirtation as a pleasure and a game, drawing people toward her for the delight of being admired, rather than out of genuine romantic intention.
